claim: Probabilistic reward learning is characterized by individual differences that become acute in aging.
source: Probabilistic reward learning is characterised by individual differences that become acute in aging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about probabilistic reward learning and aging.

claim: Age-related decline in probabilistic reward learning may be due to dopamine decline affecting neural processing in striatum, prefrontal cortex, or both.
source: This may be due to age-related dopamine (DA) decline affecting neural processing in striatum, prefrontal cortex, or both.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis in the abstract based on existing knowledge about dopamine decline in aging.

claim: Anticipatory value signals in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) were attenuated in older adults.
source: We found that anticipatory value signals in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) were attenuated in older adults.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: The strength of the vmPFC value signal predicted performance beyond age.
source: The strength of this signal predicted performance beyond age and was modulated by D1 availability in nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis showing the relationship between vmPFC signal strength and task performance.

claim: The vmPFC value signal was modulated by D1 availability in nucleus accumbens.
source: The strength of this signal predicted performance beyond age and was modulated by D1 availability in nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis correlating PET measures of D1 receptor availability with fMRI signals.

claim: A value-anticipation mechanism in vmPFC declines in aging.
source: These results uncover that a value-anticipation mechanism in vmPFC declines in aging, and that this mechanism is associated with DA D1 receptor availability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings reported in the abstract.

claim: The value-anticipation mechanism in vmPFC is associated with DA D1 receptor availability.
source: These results uncover that a value-anticipation mechanism in vmPFC declines in aging, and that this mechanism is associated with DA D1 receptor availability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between PET and fMRI measures.

claim: Older individuals are poor at probabilistic reward learning and subsequent optimal action selection compared with younger adults.
source: Compared with younger adults, older individuals are poor at probabilistic reward learning and subsequent optimal action selection (Eppinger et al., 2011; Mell et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One common account of age-related deficits in probabilistic reward learning is an age-related deterioration of the dopamine system.
source: One common account of this deficit is an age-related deterioration of the dopamine (DA) system (Volkow et al., 1998), with two of its primary targets - striatum and prefrontal cortex (PFC) - being obvious culprits.
evidence: This is presented as an established hypothesis in the field, supported by citation.

claim: DA signals from midbrain convey reward prediction errors (RPEs).
source: A wealth of animal literature demonstrates that DA signals from midbrain convey reward prediction errors (RPEs) (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Schultz et al., 1997), which are thought to act as signals that facilitate action selection in striatum (Niv and Montague, 2009; Pessiglione et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal literature.

claim: RPEs are thought to act as signals that facilitate action selection in striatum.
source: A wealth of animal literature demonstrates that DA signals from midbrain convey reward prediction errors (RPEs) (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Schultz et al., 1997), which are thought to act as signals that facilitate action selection in striatum (Niv and Montague, 2009; Pessiglione et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies reported lower correlations between RPEs and nucleus accumbens BOLD signals in older compared with younger adults.
source: Supporting this, previous studies reported lower correlations between RPEs generated from probabilistic reward learning tasks and nucleus accumbens (NAcc) BOLD signals in older compared with younger adults (Eppinger et al., 2013; Samanez-Larkin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: In older adults, neural activity in NAcc reflected only obtained reward and not expected value.
source: By decomposing RPEs in a dynamic two-armed bandit task into their two subcomponents: obtained reward (R) and expected value (Q), Chowdhury et al. (2013) showed that, in older adults, neural activity in NAcc reflected just the former.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: After pharmacological boosting of the dopaminergic system in older adults, the expected value component could be detected in NAcc.
source: Only after the dopaminergic system had been pharmacologically boosted could the expected value component be detected in NAcc.
evidence: This is a finding from Chowdhury et al. (2013) cited in the text.

claim: Age-related decline in probabilistic reward learning may be related to impaired prefrontal functioning.
source: Another hypothesis is that age-related decline in probabilistic reward learning may be related to impaired prefrontal functioning (Nyberg et al., 2010; Raz et al., 2005; Halfmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is presented as an alternative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Compromised DA projections to frontostriatal circuits are reported in aging.
source: Indeed, compromised DA projections to frontostriatal circuits are reported in aging (Dreher et al., 2008; Hämmerer and Eppinger, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Anticipatory activity reflecting the value of the chosen option in the ventromedial PFC is widely reported in decision-making tasks.
source: Anticipatory activity reflecting the value of the chosen option in the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) is widely reported in decision-making tasks (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Daw et al., 2006) and is modulated by DA (Jocham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Anticipatory activity in vmPFC is modulated by DA.
source: Anticipatory activity reflecting the value of the chosen option in the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) is widely reported in decision-making tasks (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Daw et al., 2006) and is modulated by DA (Jocham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: One previous study suggests decreased RPE signalling in vmPFC in older adults.
source: Supporting an involvement of PFC in age-related decline in probabilistic reward learning, one previous study suggests decreased RPE signalling in vmPFC in older adults (Eppinger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Within a group of older adults, increased BOLD activity related to value anticipation predicted better performance on the Iowa gambling task.
source: Another study showed that within a group of older adults with increased BOLD activity related to value anticipation predicted better performance on the Iowa gambling task (Halfmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is no published data directly showing that age-related decline in PFC value signals is related to dopaminergic deterioration.
source: However, despite evidence suggesting that age-related decline in PFC value signals could be related to dopaminergic deterioration, there is no published data directly showing this.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of evidence in the literature.

claim: Uncertainty should influence the trade-off between exploration and exploitation.
source: Uncertainty should influence the trade-off between exploration and exploitation (Sutton and Barto, 1998) that an optimal policy should balance.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by a citation.

claim: How exploration and switching are modulated in aging and how they influence performance is unclear.
source: However, how exploration and switching are modulated in aging and how they influence performance is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The study included samples of 30 older and 30 younger participants who performed a two-armed bandit task while fMRI data was acquired.
source: We included samples of 30 older and 30 younger participants who performed a two-armed bandit task (TAB) previously used by Chowdhury et al. (2013) while fMRI data was acquired.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: All participants were healthy and cognitively high functioning (MMSE > 27).
source: All participants were healthy and cognitively high functioning (MMSE > 27).
evidence: This describes the participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Participants performed 220 trials on the TAB.
source: In brief, all participants performed 220 trials on the TAB (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: On each trial, participants chose between one of two bandits, represented by fractal images.
source: On each trial, participants chose between one of two bandits, represented by fractal images.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: After a variable interval, the outcome was presented as a green arrow pointing up signalling a reward, or a yellow horizontal bar signalling no reward.
source: After a variable interval, the outcome was presented as a green arrow pointing up signalling a reward, or a yellow horizontal bar signalling no reward.
evidence: This describes the task structure.

claim: Probabilities of obtaining a reward varied over time for both bandits, according to independent Gaussian random walks.
source: Probabilities of obtaining a reward varied over time for both bandits, according to independent Gaussian random walks (Figure 1c, left).
evidence: This describes the task structure and is illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Participants received monetary earnings of 1 Swedish Krona per rewarded trial.
source: Participants received monetary earnings of 1 Swedish Krona (SEK, ~$0.11) per rewarded trial.
evidence: This describes the reward structure of the task.

claim: Behaviour was quantified with a Bayesian observer model augmented to capture the influence of variance and confidence on switch behaviour.
source: Behaviour was quantified with a Bayesian observer model augmented to capture the influence of variance and confidence on switch behaviour.
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach used.

claim: The Bayesian observer model outperformed a Rescorla-Wagner (RW) model that tracked expected value using simple RPEs.
source: This model outperformed a Rescorla-Wagner (RW) model that tracked expected value using simple RPEs.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: PET data were collected using the radioligand [11C]SCH23390 to measure striatal and prefrontal DA D1 receptor binding potential.
source: To investigate the relationship between the ability to learn about probabilistic rewards and the DA system, we collected PET data using the radioligand [11C]SCH23390 to measure striatal and prefrontal DA D1 receptor binding potential (D1 BP), as a proxy for integrity of the dopaminergic system.
evidence: This describes the PET imaging methodology.

claim: The radioligand [11C]SCH23390 allows for reliable measurement of BP in striatum and PFC simultaneously.
source: The chosen radioligand allows for reliable measurement of BP in striatum and PFC simultaneously (Hall et al., 1994), as opposed to alternative markers of dopaminergic function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Younger participants earned more money on the TAB on average than older participants.
source: Younger participants earned more money on the TAB on average (top left, t(49) = 1.69, p(one-tailed)=0.048).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Proportion of efficient choices differed significantly between younger and older groups.
source: Proportion of efficient choices differed significantly between the two groups (top right, Mann-Whitney U = 286.5, p(one-tailed)=0.029).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Number of switches did not differ significantly between age groups.
source: Number of switches did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.19; bottom left)
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The proportion of adaptive switches differed between age groups.
source: but the proportion of adaptive switches differed between age groups (bottom right, Mann-Whitney = 271.0; p(two-tailed)=0.033).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Model fit did not significantly differ between participants.
source: Model fit did not significantly differ between participants (Mann-Whitney U = 353.0, p=0.406).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: All BPs significantly differed between age groups.
source: All BPs significantly differed between groups (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Younger adults outperformed older adults on the task.
source: Younger adults outperformed older adults on the task (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There was a weak group difference in total amount of money earned (Mold = 125.9, SD = 11.4; Myoung = 130.3, SD = 8.2; t(49), p(one-tailed)=0.050).
source: There was a weak group difference in total amount of money earned (Mold = 125.9, SD = 11.4; Myoung = 130.3, SD = 8.2; t(49), p(one-tailed)=0.050).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Efficient choices differed between groups (Mold = 0.53, SD = 0.10; Myoung = 0.59. SD = 0.08, Mann-Whitney U = 286.5, p(one-tailed)=0.029).
source: Additionally, efficient choices, defined as the proportion of total choices that were more likely to be rewarded according to the actual (hidden) state of the Gaussian random walks also differed between groups (Mold = 0.53, SD = 0.10; Myoung = 0.59. SD = 0.08, Mann-Whitney U = 286.5, p(one-tailed)=0.029.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The number of switches was negatively related to total monetary gains.
source: The number of switches was negatively related to total monetary gains (r = −0.29, p=0.032, controlled for age).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: There was no evidence to suggest that the number of switches differed between age groups (Mold = 57.3, SD = 34.6; Myoung = 68.1. SD = 29.8, Mann-Whitney U = 323.0, p=0.190).
source: There was no evidence to suggest that the number of switches differed between age groups (Mold = 57.3, SD = 34.6; Myoung = 68.1. SD = 29.8, Mann-Whitney U = 323.0, p=0.190).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The winning model was the Bayesian observer model with five parameters.
source: The winning model, defined as the model with the lowest integrated BIC (iBIC), was the Bayesian observer model with five parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison shown in Table 1.

claim: No single model parameter differed between age groups.
source: No single model parameter differed between age groups (Mann-Whitney test: β, U = 386.0, p=0.761; ω, U = 345.0, p=0.338; λ, U = 401.0, p=0.949; υ, U = 307.0, p=0.117; κ, U = 374.0, p=0.620).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of model parameters.

claim: A multivariate analysis with the model parameters as independent variables and age group as a fixed factor did not yield any significant predictor of age group.
source: A multivariate analysis with the model parameters as independent variables and age group as a fixed factor did not yield any significant predictor of age group (F = 0.91, p=0.482).
evidence: This is a finding from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Model fit did not differ between age groups (Mann-Whitney U = 353.0, p=0.406).
source: Model fit, defined by the individual log likelihood for each participant, also did not differ between age groups (Mann-Whitney U = 353.0, p=0.406).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: In the best-performing RW model, younger participants learned more quickly.
source: In the best-performing RW model (which fit the behavioural data less well), younger participants learned more quickly (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from model analysis reported in supplementary materials.

claim: Young participants had a higher proportion of adaptive switches compared with old participants (Mold = 57.4, SD = 23.4; Myoung = 68.3. SD = 18.2, Mann-Whitney test U = 271.5, p=0.033).
source: We used the expected values from the winning model to assess the proportion of adaptive switches (to subjectively better bandits) versus maladaptive switches (to subjectively worse bandits) and found that young participants had a higher proportion of adaptive switches compared with old participants (Mold = 57.4, SD = 23.4; Myoung = 68.3. SD = 18.2, Mann-Whitney test U = 271.5, p=0.033, Figure 1b, bottom right).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The proportion of adaptive switches was positively associated with total monetary gains (r(54) = 0.49, p<0.001).
source: The proportion of adaptive switches was positively associated with total monetary gains (r(54) = 0.49, p<0.001), suggesting that the age difference in performance partly resulted from differences in strategic switching.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The age difference in performance partly resulted from differences in strategic switching.
source: The proportion of adaptive switches was positively associated with total monetary gains (r(54) = 0.49, p<0.001), suggesting that the age difference in performance partly resulted from differences in strategic switching.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between adaptive switches and performance.

claim: Clusters in vmPFC, bilateral hippocampus, visual cortex and bilateral precuneus showed a positive correlation between BOLD and Q at the time of choice at p(FWE-corrected)<0.05.
source: Clusters in vmPFC, bilateral hippocampus, visual cortex and bilateral precuneus showed a positive correlation between BOLD and Q at the time of choice at p(FWE-corrected)<0.05 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis.

claim: Younger participants showed a stronger representation of Q in vmPFC compared to the older participants (Mold = 2.84, SD = 5.25; Myoung = 6.44, SD = 6.07; t(55) = 2.38; p=0.021).
source: A two-sample t-test, orthogonal to the test used to define this ROI, revealed that younger participants showed a stronger representation of Q in vmPFC compared to the older participants (Mold = 2.84, SD = 5.25; Myoung = 6.44, SD = 6.07; t(55) = 2.38; p=0.021).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The difference in vmPFC value signal did not arise because of the difference in learning performance.
source: This difference in vmPFC value signal did not arise because of the difference in learning performance: when we restricted our analysis to high performers as defined by a median split (13 old, 15 young), a difference in performance was no longer significant (p=0.60), but the strength of expected-value signal in vmPFC was correlated with age (r(26) = −0.39, p=0.040) and we found a marginally significant difference between age groups (Mold = 4.21, SD = 4.81; Myoung = 8.29, SD = 5.72; t(26) = 2.03, p=0.054).
evidence: This is a finding from a subgroup analysis controlling for performance.

claim: On average, the expected-value signal was stronger and sustained for longer throughout the trial in younger compared with older adults.
source: This suggests that, on average, the expected-value signal was stronger and sustained for longer throughout the trial in younger compared with older adults (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is an observation from time-course analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The parameter estimate for Q in vmPFC was positively related to total monetary gains (r(53)=0.37, p=0.006, controlling for age and model fit).
source: The parameter estimate for Q in vmPFC was positively related to total monetary gains (r(53)=0.37, p=0.006, controlling for age and model fit in a partial correlation).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Q in vmPFC was a significant predictor of all measures of performance.
source: Q in vmPFC was a significant predictor of all measures of performance (bivariate correlations: total monetary gains: r(55) = 0.47, p<0.001 adaptive switches: r(55) = 0.39, p=0.003; efficient choices: r(55) = 0.38, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Age was a significant predictor of all measures of performance.
source: Age was also a significant predictor of all measures of performance (bivariate correlations: total monetary gains: r(55) = -0.32, p=0.050; adaptive switches: r(55) = -0.26 p=0.052; efficient choices: r(55) = -0.32 p=0.015).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Age was a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC (r(55) = -0.32 p=0.016).
source: Age was also a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC (r(55) = -0.32 p=0.016).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Age was no longer a significant predictor of performance after controlling for Q in vmPFC.
source: Age was no longer a significant predictor of performance after controlling for Q in vmPFC (beta age = −0.12,–0.23, and −0.15; p=0.328, 0.086 and 0.255, for monetary gains, efficient choices and adaptive switches, respectively), whereas Q in vmPFC remained a significant predictor of all measures of performance (beta Q in vmPFC = 0.43, 0.30, and 0.34; p=0.001, 0.023 and 0.012 for monetary gains, efficient choices and adaptive switches, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis.

claim: The findings are consistent with a full mediation of age effects on performance by Q in vmPFC.
source: This is consistent with a full mediation of age effects on performance by Q in vmPFC.
evidence: This is an inference from the regression analysis results.

claim: It is difficult to make inferences on mediation effects of age in a cross-sectional dataset.
source: Note, however, that it is difficult to make inferences on mediation effects of age in a cross-sectional dataset (Lindenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological caveat supported by citation.

claim: RPEs are widely reported in NAcc.
source: RPEs are widely reported in NAcc (Behrens et al., 2008; Niv et al., 2012); but see also (Stenner et al., 2015; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by citations.

claim: RPEs are thought to be a critical signal conveyed by dopaminergic neurons.
source: RPEs are thought to be a critical signal conveyed by dopaminergic neurons (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Hart et al., 2014) that guide action selection in probabilistic learning tasks (Pessiglione et al., 2006; Hart et al., 2014; Rolls et al., 2008) like the TAB.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: RPEs guide action selection in probabilistic learning tasks.
source: RPEs are thought to be a critical signal conveyed by dopaminergic neurons (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Hart et al., 2014) that guide action selection in probabilistic learning tasks (Pessiglione et al., 2006; Hart et al., 2014; Rolls et al., 2008) like the TAB.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: The study replicated previous findings in older adults showing a significant effect of R but no significant negative effect of Q in NAcc.
source: We replicated previous findings in older adults (Chowdhury et al., 2013), as we saw a significant effect of R, but no significant negative effect of Q in both ROIs (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Contrary to the hypothesis, a canonical prediction error was not observed in the young sample either.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not observe a canonical prediction error in the young sample either.
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI analysis that contradicts the initial hypothesis.

claim: No evidence for differences between the different age groups' mean activation for R or Q were found (p>0.29).
source: No evidence for differences between the different age groups' mean activation for R or Q were found (p>0.29).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: When extracting parameter estimates for the full RPE (R-Q), no differences between the groups' mean activation were observed (p>0.45).
source: In addition, when performing a less stringent test and extracting parameter estimates from this ROI for the full RPE, defined as one regressor (R-Q), we did not observe any differences between the groups' mean activation (p>0.45).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The negative results were not dependent on using the Bayesian observer model to generate Q.
source: These negative results were not dependent on using the Bayesian observer model to generate Q as they were consistent across models (Supporting figure to Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: There was no indication that the lack of expected value signal in the NAcc at the group level was caused by some participants showing poor learning of expected value.
source: There was no indication that the lack of expected value signal in the NAcc at the group level was caused by some participants showing poor learning of expected value, as the correlation between Q in NAcc and the different measures of performance (monetary gains, effective choices, and adaptive switches) was not significant (p>0.25).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The RW model generated better predictions of the BOLD signal in NAcc than the Bayesian observer model.
source: The RW model generated better predictions of the BOLD signal in NAcc (paired t-test comparing residuals of the respective GLM models within functional ROIs; t(56) = 5.69, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The Bayesian observer model generates better predictions of the BOLD signal in the vmPFC than the RW model.
source: On the other hand, the Bayesian observer model generates better predictions of the BOLD signal in the vmPFC when Q as generated by each model was included as a parametric modulator at the time of choice (paired t-test comparing residuals of the respective GLM models across all voxels in the respective vmPFC ROIs; t(56) = 5.62, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: Younger participants had higher values for binding potentials in all ROIs considered (p<0.001 in all seven ROIs).
source: Younger participants had higher values for binding potentials in all ROIs considered (p<0.001 in all seven ROIs, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from PET data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BP in none of the ROIs was correlated with any measure of performance or any of the model parameters after controlling for multiple comparisons.
source: BP in none of the ROIs was correlated with any measure of performance or any of the model parameters after controlling for multiple comparisons (p>0.02; adjusted threshold when controlling for 42 comparisons: p=0.001, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: D1 BP among ROIs was highly correlated after controlling for age (r(53) = 0.411–0.911, p<0.001).
source: D1 BP among ROIs was highly correlated after controlling for age (r(53) = 0.411–0.911, p<0.001, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: BP in NAcc and putamen were related to Q in vmPFC after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: BP in NAcc and putamen were related to Q in vmPFC after correcting for multiple comparisons (corrected threshold considering seven ROIs p=0.007; NAcc: r(56) = 0.41, p=0.002; putamen: r(56) = 0.36, p=0.006).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: When controlling for age, the correlation between BP in NAcc and Q in vmPFC survived (r(53) = 0.28 p=0.038).
source: When controlling for age as a predictor of no interest, this correlation only survived for NAcc (r(53) = 0.28 p=0.038, Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a finding from partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Age was a significant predictor of both BP in NAcc (r(54) = -0.78, p<0.001) and Q in vmPFC (r(55) = -0.32, p=0.016).
source: Age was a significant predictor of both BP in NAcc (r(54) = -0.78, p<0.001) and Q in vmPFC (r(55) = -0.32, p=0.016).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: BP in Nacc was a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC r(54)=0.41, p=0.001.
source: BP in Nacc was also a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC r(54)=0.41, p=0.001.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Age was no longer a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC after controlling for BP in NAcc (beta age = −0.01, p=0.964; beta BP in NAcc = 0.42, p=0.038).
source: Age was no longer a significant predictor of Q in vmPFC after controlling for BP in NAcc (beta age = −0.01, p=0.964; beta BP in NAcc = 0.42, p=0.038).
evidence: This is a finding from regression analysis.

claim: The findings are consistent with a full mediation of age effects on Q in vmPFC by DA D1 BP in NAcc.
source: This is consistent with a full mediation of age effects on Q in vmPFC by DA D1 BP in NAcc.
evidence: This is an inference from the regression analysis results.

claim: There was no significant interaction between age group and NAcc D1 BP in modelling Q in vmPFC.
source: Further, despite the main effect of age on D1 BP in NAcc, there was no significant interaction between age group and NAcc D1 BP (F(1,52) = 1.20; p=0.279) in modelling Q in vmPFC; thus, the relationship between DA D1 BP in NAcc and Q in vmPFC did not differ between age groups.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis.

claim: No significant relationship was found between the representation of Q in NAcc at outcome time and D1 BP in any of the ROIs examined.
source: We did not find any significant relationship between the representation of Q in NAcc at outcome time and D1 BP in any of the ROIs examined (p>0.11 in bivariate correlations; p>0.13 when controlling for age).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Value anticipation in vmPFC predicted performance beyond age and was attenuated in older participants.
source: We also showed that value anticipation in vmPFC predicted performance beyond age and was attenuated in older participants.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: The value signal in vmPFC was modulated by D1 BP in NAcc.
source: Furthermore, the value signal in vmPFC was modulated by D1 BP in NAcc.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: The computational model showed that the tendency for choice perseveration can be described as aversion to the variance of the unchosen option.
source: Finally, our computational model showed that the tendency for choice perseveration can be described as aversion to the variance of the unchosen option and that, for most participants, greater subjective confidence in a previous choice promoted switches away from that choice.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling analysis.

claim: For most participants, greater subjective confidence in a previous choice promoted switches away from that choice.
source: Finally, our computational model showed that the tendency for choice perseveration can be described as aversion to the variance of the unchosen option and that, for most participants, greater subjective confidence in a previous choice promoted switches away from that choice.
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling analysis.

claim: An age-related impairment in probabilistic reward learning has been widely reported.
source: An age-related impairment in probabilistic reward learning has been widely reported (Mell et al., 2005; Eppinger et al., 2013; Chowdhury et al., 2013; Eppinger et al., 2015; Samanez-Larkin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by citations.

claim: The age-related deterioration of the dopaminergic system has been hypothesised to underlie age-related cognitive decline.
source: The age-related deterioration of the dopaminergic system (Volkow et al., 1998) has been hypothesised to underlie age-related cognitive decline (Volkow et al., 1998; Bäckman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: One mechanism through which DA deficits can affect probabilistic learning performance in aging is by attenuation of value signals in the brain.
